Same shape: credit-header identity resolution, address history, relatives and associates, assets, court and licence records, all source-dated. www.accurint.com is the customer product portal; risk.lexisnexis.com is the corporate site and does not carry an Accurint product page. Because both draw on overlapping upstream files, a match in CLEAR and in Accurint is NOT independent corroboration.

name: libphonenumber
jurisdiction_notes: Fully offline. No data leaves the machine and no third party learns which number you looked at. Safest possible first step on a phone selector.
notes: Google's phone metadata library and the reference implementation for parsing, validating and normalising to E.164, with region, timezone and carrier mapping from the numbering plan. Authoritative on what a number CAN be; it cannot tell you whether the number is assigned. Graded B not A because the metadata is a curated third-party copy of regulator-published numbering plans and lags allocation changes — pin the library version in your notes. Ported numbers keep the original allocation prefix, so treat carrier output as the original allocation and not the current carrier.

name: LinkedIn
jurisdiction_notes: hiQ v. LinkedIn narrowed CFAA exposure for scraping public profiles, but LinkedIn's user agreement still forbids it and the breach-of-contract route survived, so scraping remains legally exposed. Employment history on EU and UK subjects is personal data.
notes: ACTIVE BY DEFAULT: viewing a profile notifies its owner unless you are in private browsing mode, and private mode disables your own who-viewed-me data. This is the single most common way an investigator tips off a corporate target. Prefer a logged-out view or a search engine's site: operator. Content is self-asserted — B evidence of what the person CLAIMS, C evidence of fact.

name: Maigret
jurisdiction_notes: Same enumeration exposure as Sherlock, plus it parses hit pages, which is scraping under most platform ToS.
notes: Sherlock-derived but parses matched profile pages and extracts names, bios, ids and sometimes emails, so it produces pivots rather than a bare URL list. Emits HTML and PDF reports. Recursive search on discovered ids widens scope fast; cap it against the case question.

name: NeverBounce
jurisdiction_notes: SMTP probing of a third party's mail server. Inside an authorised engagement this is fine; outside one it is unsolicited traffic to infrastructure you do not own.
notes: Deliverability verification: syntax, MX presence, catch-all detection and an SMTP RCPT check. ACTIVE — the check connects to the target domain's mail server and the connection lands in that server's logs, which can tip off a security team. Catch-all domains return inconclusive, not negative. Trial credits exist but real use is paid. Use only when deliverability is genuinely the question.

name: North Carolina Voter Registration Data
jurisdiction_notes: North Carolina publishes the statewide voter registration file and voter history as bulk downloads under state public-records law. This is jurisdiction-specific: US state voter files range from freely downloadable, through restricted to political committees, to barred for commercial use entirely. Never assume another state matches — confirm the receiving state's rules before requesting or using a file.
notes: Primary state record and one of the most openly published voter files in the US. Gives registered name, residential and mailing address, age range, registration date, party and precinct, plus per-election participation history — excellent for an address timeline or testing a residency claim. Sensitive identifiers such as SSN and driver licence number are withheld. The endpoint is the voter registration data page itself, under the board's results and data section.

name: Numverify
jurisdiction_notes: The provider learns which number you queried. Free-tier terms have historically restricted the free plan to plain HTTP, which would expose the queried number in transit — check the current plan terms before use.
notes: Hosted validation returning validity, country, location, carrier and line type from a database rather than a live network query. Convenient wrapper over what libphonenumber already gives you offline, plus a carrier field. apilayer-operated, small free tier. Carrier data suffers the same number-porting problem as any prefix-derived lookup.

name: OpenAlex
rate_limit: unknown; higher limits are offered to callers who supply a contact email
jurisdiction_notes: Fully open bibliographic data under CC0. Successor to the discontinued Microsoft Academic Graph.
notes: Open scholarly index of works, authors and institutions with a free API and no key requirement, which makes it the automatable alternative to Google Scholar. Author disambiguation is algorithmic and imperfect on common names — expect both split and merged author records. Institution linkage is good enough to test a claimed affiliation.

name: ORCID
jurisdiction_notes: Researchers publish these records deliberately. Fields may be marked private by the holder; only the public view is fair game.
notes: Persistent researcher identifier resolving to employment history, education, funding and publications. Excellent for disambiguating common names in academia and for testing a claimed affiliation or doctorate during due diligence. Grade the layers separately: the identifier and its linked works are B, but most employment and education fields are self-asserted by the holder and are C at best. Entries asserted by the institution itself are flagged as such in the record and are the ones worth citing.

name: PhoneInfoga
jurisdiction_notes: Numbering-plan analysis is neutral, but the search-engine scanners it drives put the number into third-party query logs.
notes: Numbering-plan parsing (country, area, line type) plus scanners that pivot the number into search engines and reverse-lookup sites. Local reconnaissance only — it does not dial or message the number. Several bundled scanners need their own API keys and silently no-op without them, so check which scanners actually ran before recording a negative.

name: Pipl
jurisdiction_notes: Closed its free consumer search in 2019 and now sells only to identity-verification, fraud and investigative customers under contractual use restrictions. Non-FCRA. Access is gated on a stated permissible use, so expect to justify the engagement.
notes: Identity-resolution service linking email, phone, username and name into a single person record; notably better than consumer aggregators at username-to-person because it indexes profile data rather than only public records. Now positioned primarily as enterprise fraud and risk intelligence rather than an investigator lookup, so confirm the search product you need is still sold separately. Sourcing is disclosed per field and confidence is scored, which is better than its consumer peers, but it remains an aggregator and aggregation is not corroboration.

name: PubMed
jurisdiction_notes: US National Library of Medicine primary index, public and free to query.
notes: Authoritative for the biomedical publication record. In due diligence it is the fastest way to test a claimed clinical or research career, and author affiliation strings give employer history with dates. Retraction notices are indexed and linked, which matters when assessing a subject's credibility. Biomedical coverage only — absence says nothing about other fields.

name: Reddit
jurisdiction_notes: Public profile pages are viewable without an account and without notifying the user. Usernames are frequently pseudonymous and frequently reused across platforms — a name match is not an identification.
notes: A user page lists post and comment history with timestamps, the richest free source of routine, timezone and interest signals attached to a username. OPERATIONAL: robots.txt now disallows every user-agent and the Public Content Policy restricts reuse, and the site serves a bot-verification interstitial to non-browser clients, so expect manual browsing rather than scripted fetches. Deleted content is gone from the live site, so check archives. Pushshift, which made historical Reddit fully searchable, lost public access after the 2023 API changes — assume gaps in any historical query.

name: RocketReach
jurisdiction_notes: US sales-intelligence data broker. Not an FCRA consumer reporting agency, so output must not be used for employment, tenancy, credit or insurance decisions. EU and UK subjects hold erasure rights against it.
notes: Contact-data aggregator over scraped profiles and partner feeds. Useful for corporate email and direct-dial discovery on a named individual at a named employer. D reliability: it aggregates other aggregators, records go stale, and aggregation is not corroboration — a hit is only evidence that a broker asserts a link.

name: Sherlock
jurisdiction_notes: Probes several hundred third-party platforms directly from your IP. Automated account enumeration is contested under some platform ToS and some computer-misuse statutes. Run it from scoped egress, not from a client network.
notes: Open-source CLI username enumerator. Triage, not evidence: high false positives on sites that return 200 for every path, and false negatives where a platform blocks datacentre IPs. Confirm every hit by opening the profile yourself. Site list drifts, re-pull before a case.

name: Spokeo
jurisdiction_notes: US in practice. NOT an FCRA consumer reporting agency — output must not be used for employment, tenancy, credit, insurance or any other FCRA-covered eligibility decision. Spokeo v. Robins is the leading US authority on standing to sue an aggregator over inaccurate records. CCPA and CPRA give California residents deletion rights, which matters in self-audit work.
notes: Consumer people-search over public records, marketing data and social profiles. D reliability and it matters: it merges records on weak keys, so a single report routinely blends two different people. ITS AGGREGATION IS NOT CORROBORATION — five aggregators agreeing normally means they bought the same upstream file. Generate a lead here, then verify against a primary record.

name: ThatsThem
jurisdiction_notes: US only, non-FCRA, free. The reverse-email and reverse-IP features surface data the subject almost certainly did not knowingly publish — check the case question actually reaches that far before using them.
notes: Free aggregator whose advantage over its peers is the breadth of accepted selectors: name, address, phone, email and IP all resolve into the same record set. The site now promotes a free registration for instant access, so confirm whether unauthenticated search still returns full records before relying on it. It states it draws on over fifty upstream sources — aggregation is not corroboration, and a second opinion here on a Spokeo or Whitepages hit is likely the same upstream file restated. Its IP-to-household mapping is marketing-derived and frequently wrong.

name: Thomson Reuters CLEAR
jurisdiction_notes: US. Requires a credentialed account and a declared GLBA and DPPA permissible purpose; motor-vehicle and credit-header data are restricted by federal statute and misuse is personal legal exposure, not merely a contract breach. Every search is logged and auditable, and those logs are discoverable.
notes: Investigator-grade aggregator over credit headers, court records, liens, licences, vehicles and corporate filings. Far better sourced than consumer people-search: each element carries a source and a date range, so a report can be unpicked back to a primary record — do that, and cite the primary record, because aggregation is not corroboration and its own output advises verification. Standard tooling in US corporate due diligence and fraud work.

name: Truecaller
jurisdiction_notes: Its database is built from users uploading their own address books, so most entries describe people who never consented; it has drawn data-protection scrutiny in the EU and India. Installing the app to run a search will upload YOUR contacts, a disclosure of third-party data you are probably not entitled to make. Use a clean device or do not use it.
notes: Crowdsourced reverse phone lookup with strong coverage in South Asia, the Middle East and parts of Africa where commercial lookups return nothing. ACTIVE — the premium who-viewed-my-profile feature surfaces searchers to the person being searched, and suppressing that requires the searcher's own premium incognito mode, so a logged-in search can tip off the target exactly the way a LinkedIn profile view does. A name here is whatever other users saved the number as, so it can be a nickname, a stale label or a smear; aggregation is not corroboration and a Truecaller name is never an identification on its own.

name: TruePeopleSearch
jurisdiction_notes: US only, free, ad-supported, non-FCRA. Because it is free and unauthenticated it is the first place a harasser looks, so filing an opt-out here is a standard deliverable in a self-audit engagement.
notes: Free reverse lookup on name, phone or address returning current and prior addresses, age, and named relatives and associates. Prior-address coverage is genuinely good for building an address timeline. D reliability, no sourcing shown at all, and the relative graph includes people who merely shared an address at some point. Aggregation is not corroboration.

name: Twilio Lookup
jurisdiction_notes: Caller-name (CNAM) data is US-centric and its use is constrained by carrier agreements. Some Lookup packages query carrier systems and leave a record on the carrier side, though nothing reaches the subscriber.
notes: The most reliable commercially available line-type and carrier lookup, because it resolves against carrier databases rather than prefix guesses and therefore handles ported numbers correctly. CNAM returns a registered caller name for many US landline and mobile numbers, which is a genuine name pivot. Priced per lookup per package.

name: UK Register of Electors
jurisdiction_notes: Two registers exist and the distinction is the whole point. The OPEN (edited) register is sold to anyone and is what commercial lookup services resell. The FULL register may lawfully be used only for elections, law enforcement, credit referencing and other prescribed purposes, and is inspectable only under supervision at the local authority without copying. Using full-register data outside a prescribed purpose is an offence. Individuals may opt out of the open register, so absence proves nothing.
notes: Authoritative UK name-to-address record. The endpoint is the GOV.UK guidance page that explains the two registers and points to the local-authority route; there is no national online lookup. In practice you reach the open register through a commercial reseller and the full register through a permitted-purpose route or supervised council inspection. Registers are compiled locally, so you need the right council. Rolling registration means the published version lags a move by weeks.

name: WhatsMyName
jurisdiction_notes: The web UI issues the probe requests from the analyst's own browser, so each platform sees your IP and browser fingerprint rather than a shared service's.
notes: Detection ruleset (wmn-data.json) maintained by OSINT Combine and contributors, consumed by many other username tools; the JSON list is the real asset and can be used offline. Better curated than Sherlock's list and records a per-site account-exists indicator. Still triage-grade, confirm each hit manually.

name: Whitepages
jurisdiction_notes: Same FCRA prohibition as any people-search: not for employment, tenancy, credit or insurance decisions. Offers an opt-out, which is a standard deliverable step in a self-audit engagement.
notes: Oldest of the US directory aggregators, strongest on the phone-to-address-to-name triangle and on identifying landlines and household composition. Free tier shows partial results, full report is paid. Same D-grade merging problem as all aggregators — aggregation is not corroboration, so treat every reported relative and associate as an unverified assertion.

name: X (formerly Twitter)
jurisdiction_notes: Posts are self-published by the account holder and viewing does not notify them. Bulk collection about EU and UK subjects remains personal-data processing however public the posts are. The twitter.com domain redirects to x.com, and older links, embeds and archived references still carry the old host.
notes: The strongest free operator set on any social platform, exposed through the advanced search form: from:, to:, since: and until: with YYYY-MM-DD dates, filter:media, filter:links and filter:replies with a leading minus to invert, lang:, url:, min_faves:, min_retweets: and min_replies:, and list:. filter:verified survived but its meaning did not - since verification became a paid subscription it no longer indicates identity verification and is worthless as an authenticity signal. Logged-out browsing and search were closed off in 2023, so an account is required and that account is itself an exposure: reading does not notify the target, but it does feed the recommendation graph, which can surface you in the target's suggestions. Bot protection defeats scripted fetching - use a browser. Deleted posts vanish from the site, so pivot to the web archives. Content is self-asserted: B evidence of what the account claimed and when, C evidence of fact.

name: Amass
rate_limit: depends on the data sources you configure
notes: OWASP subdomain enumeration and network mapping. Marked active because default operation resolves candidate names and brute-forces, which touches target infrastructure; it does have a passive-only mode, and you must select it deliberately. Most of its value comes from third-party API keys you supply.

name: APNIC Whois
rate_limit: queries are throttled to protect personal data
jurisdiction_notes: Asia-Pacific service region.
notes: Primary registry for Asia-Pacific allocations, same object model as RIPE. Many records refer down to a national NIR such as JPNIC, KRNIC or CNNIC that holds the finer-grained assignment - follow the referral instead of stopping at the APNIC-level record.

name: ARIN Whois-RWS
jurisdiction_notes: North America and parts of the Caribbean.
notes: ARIN RDAP and Whois-RWS search. Authoritative for North American allocations and returns organisation records, POC handles and - critically - the customer records for reassigned sub-blocks, which often name the downstream user rather than the ISP that holds the parent block.

name: BuiltWith
notes: Technology profile of a site drawn from BuiltWith own crawl, plus the pivot that actually matters: reverse lookup by analytics identifier, ad-network ID or tracking code to find every other site sharing it. That reverse lookup is a paid feature. Crawl-based, so entries lag reality and dead technologies linger. Wappalyzer covers similar ground but has moved largely behind payment.

name: Censys Search
notes: Internet-wide scan data plus a strong certificate index; you read Censys snapshots, so the target observes nothing. Best used for certificate-field pivots - subject organisation, SAN lists - and for finding hosts a domain used to point at. Free access has been progressively restricted; expect an account and a low query cap. Marked unverified because both search.censys.io and platform.censys.io answer automated requests with a bot-protection interstitial; the corporate site at censys.com does respond, so confirm the current search entry point in a browser before scripting against it.

name: CIRCL Passive DNS
jurisdiction_notes: EU (Luxembourg) operator; access granted case by case to vetted requesters.
notes: Passive DNS run by the Luxembourg national CERT. Not an open service - credentials are issued to CSIRTs, researchers and other vetted parties, which fits threat-intel and DFIR work but rarely ad hoc journalism. Strong European coverage. CIRCL also runs a separate passive SSL service on the same site.

name: Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 DNS over HTTPS
notes: RFC 8484 DoH endpoint; also answers a JSON form with name and type parameters when the request carries an application/dns-json accept header, confirmed live. A bare GET returns 400, which is correct behaviour and not an outage. Worth querying alongside Google Public DNS: geo-steered and split-horizon zones return different answers to different resolvers, and the difference is itself a finding. Same active caveat - the query ends up at the target nameservers.

name: crt.sh
notes: Searchable mirror of the public Certificate Transparency logs and the single best zero-key subdomain source: every publicly trusted TLS certificate issued for a name lands here. Blind spots are structural - wildcard certificates hide the specific hostname, and internal hosts that never got a public certificate never appear. Operated by Sectigo; large-estate queries frequently time out.

name: dig (BIND DNS utilities)
notes: Local CLI and the reference client. Direct observation of the live zone: A, AAAA, MX, NS, TXT, SOA, CAA and PTR. Querying the target own nameservers directly is the most detectable form of DNS lookup - go through a public resolver when that matters. Windows equivalents: nslookup or Resolve-DnsName.

name: DNSDB (DomainTools Farsight)
notes: Large commercial passive DNS built from real recursive-resolver observations - the reference dataset for historical resolution and for finding every name that ever pointed at an IP. Farsight Security was acquired by DomainTools in 2021 and the product now sits under the DomainTools brand; older farsightsecurity.com links and standalone tooling from pre-2021 guides may no longer work as documented.

name: DNSDumpster
rate_limit: free tier is capped per day
notes: Free subdomain and DNS map operated by HackerTarget. Its subdomain discovery is drawn from collected open-source data rather than brute force, but the record view it returns for a submitted domain is current, and there is no public documentation establishing that every field comes from a stored snapshot. Graded active on that uncertainty: if it does resolve at query time, the target authoritative nameservers see a lookup from HackerTarget infrastructure, not from you. Coverage is shallow next to certificate-transparency enumeration; use it as a first pass, never as the complete answer. API access requires an account.

name: DomainTools
notes: The deepest historical WHOIS archive plus reverse WHOIS by registrant name, email or phone - the primary way to tie a set of domains to one registrant across time. Expensive with no meaningful free tier. The pre-GDPR historical records are the highest-value part, because that data is redacted everywhere else today.

name: FOFA
jurisdiction_notes: Operated from China; queries, account details and payment data fall under Chinese jurisdiction.
notes: Internet asset search with markedly better coverage of Chinese and other Asian infrastructure than Shodan or Censys - worth a second pass whenever a target hosts in that region. Weigh the jurisdiction before submitting a sensitive selector to it.

name: Google Public DNS
notes: DoH and JSON resolver; the JSON form at /resolve with name and type parameters was confirmed returning a live answer. Resolution reaches the target authoritative nameservers through Google recursive infrastructure, so treat it as active - though the target sees a Google resolver IP, not yours. Accepts an IP for PTR (reverse DNS) lookups.

name: GreyNoise
notes: Answers one narrow question well: is this IP opportunistic internet background noise or is it aimed at you specifically. The fastest way to discard an alert or an IP before spending hours attributing it. It will not tell you who owns the host - pivot to an RIR for that.

name: Hurricane Electric BGP Toolkit
notes: Free and fast: ASN to announced prefixes, prefix to origin ASN, peers, upstreams, and the DNS names HE has observed inside a netblock. Standard first stop for what else does this organisation announce. Routing and peering data is solid; the DNS-names-in-prefix view is best-effort and incomplete.

name: IANA RDAP Bootstrap Registry
notes: Authoritative machine-readable files mapping TLDs, IPv4 and IPv6 ranges and ASN ranges to the RDAP base URL that actually serves them. The directory listing was confirmed to contain dns.json, ipv4.json, ipv6.json, asn.json and object-tags.json. This is how you find the correct registry endpoint for any object instead of guessing - including all five RIRs, so LACNIC and AFRINIC objects are reachable from here without a separate row. No key, no throttle.

name: ICANN Lookup
jurisdiction_notes: Registrant contact fields for most gTLDs are redacted under GDPR; unredacted data normally requires a documented request to the registrar.
notes: ICANN own registration data lookup. Authoritative for registrar, EPP status codes, nameservers and dates even when the contact block is redacted. Creation date, registrar transfers and status codes are usually more evidentially useful than the redacted contacts anyway. Served as a JavaScript application, so scripted retrieval gets a shell page - use RDAP for machine-readable output.

name: IPinfo.io
notes: IP context: ASN, carrier, and hosting, VPN and proxy flags plus coarse geolocation. The privacy-service flags are the genuinely valuable part - they tell you an address is a commercial VPN exit before you build a theory on its apparent country. Same accuracy caveats as any GeoIP dataset.

name: LeakIX
jurisdiction_notes: Indexes exposed data and misconfigured services; retrieving exposed content beyond metadata may be unlawful in some jurisdictions even where the index itself is public.
notes: Search over hosts with exposed services and open databases. In an authorised assessment it shows what is already public about the client estate. Read the metadata, not the exposed contents - pulling leaked data is outside passive collection and outside almost every engagement scope.

name: MaxMind GeoLite2
notes: Free downloadable country, city and ASN databases. Since 2019 a registered account and licence key are required even for the free files. City accuracy is poor and coordinates are frequently the centroid of a country or region rather than a real place - never present a GeoIP coordinate as a location finding about a person.

name: Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence (PassiveTotal)
notes: RiskIQ PassiveTotal was absorbed into Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence and the free community tier that most older OSINT guides reference has been withdrawn - community.riskiq.com no longer serves it. Access now depends on a Microsoft licence, so this is a paid source with no free path in. Still among the better passive DNS, host-pair and tracker-ID datasets if the licence is available to you. Marked unverified because the host redirects straight into a Microsoft sign-in flow whose return address is the Defender portal - the destination is plainly Microsoft, but nothing behind the login could be observed to confirm this is the MDTI entry point.

name: MXToolbox
rate_limit: free tier limited; paid plans add monitoring
notes: Web front end for MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC and blacklist checks. Fastest route from a domain to its mail provider and to the third parties authorised in SPF, which frequently names CRM, marketing and ticketing vendors. Performs live lookups, so it is active; results are not published.

name: Nmap
jurisdiction_notes: Unauthorised port scanning is a criminal offence in several jurisdictions; scan only assets named in a written scope.
notes: Direct observation - the authoritative answer for what is listening right now, and the reference implementation for service and version detection. Fully active: packets originate from your host and appear in the target logs with your source address. Requires active_allowed in scope plus a fresh confirmation naming the specific host set.

name: PeeringDB
notes: Network operators self-published interconnection records: facilities, internet exchange points, traffic levels and NOC contacts. The most direct route from an ASN to physical data-centre locations and named operational staff. Graded C because every record is a self-report by the network itself with no registry verification, and stale entries are common - a PeeringDB facility is a claim by the operator, not an established fact. Some fields require a logged-in account.

name: Qualys SSL Labs Server Test
notes: Thorough TLS configuration and certificate-chain assessment. Two gotchas that matter operationally: it connects to the target from Qualys infrastructure, and results are added to a public board unless you tick the option to hide them - so a careless test publishes the fact that someone is examining the target.

name: RDAP.org
notes: Redirector that routes an RDAP query to the correct registry using the IANA bootstrap, so you do not have to know which registry holds the object. A live domain query was observed redirecting to the registry own RDAP server, which is the behaviour to expect and the reason this is a router rather than a dataset. Returns structured JSON where legacy WHOIS returns unparseable free text. Third-party operated - for evidentiary work, follow the redirect and quote the registry own response. The homepage itself redirects to about.rdap.org; the query paths remain on rdap.org.

name: RIPE Atlas
notes: Global probe network for traceroute, ping and DNS measurements. Active twice over: real packets reach the target from real hosts, and the measurement definition is publicly visible on Atlas, which can disclose your interest in a target to anyone watching. Reading other people existing public measurement results is passive and often enough.

name: RIPE Database
rate_limit: personal-data queries are throttled per source IP per day
jurisdiction_notes: Covers Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia. Personal data in the database is subject to GDPR and to the RIPE database acceptable-use terms - bulk extraction of contact objects is prohibited.
notes: Primary registry for allocations in the RIPE region. The inetnum, route, aut-num and abuse-c objects give registered holder, maintainer and abuse contact. Registered holder is not the operator: large blocks are routinely sub-assigned, and the more specific object is the one that names the real user.

name: RIPEstat
notes: RIPE NCC data portal over registry and routing data: announced prefixes, ASN neighbours, routing history from the RIS collectors, abuse contacts and blocklist observations. Coverage is global, not limited to the RIPE service region, and RIPE NCC operates much of the underlying measurement itself. A documented public data API exists.

name: SecurityTrails
rate_limit: free tier is a small monthly query quota
notes: Historical DNS and historical WHOIS plus reverse lookup by nameserver, MX record and WHOIS field. One of the few practical answers to what did this domain resolve to two years ago. The free tier has been repeatedly reduced - confirm the current quota before planning a case around it. Marked unverified because the host answers automated requests with a bot-protection interstitial rather than the site, so the endpoint could not be confirmed from evidence; open it in a browser before relying on it.

name: Shodan
rate_limit: credits per plan; free accounts are heavily limited
notes: Queryable index of Shodan own internet-wide scans - you read their snapshot and the target sees nothing. Banners, TLS certificates, exposed services, screenshots. Supports favicon pivoting through the http.favicon.hash filter, which surfaces every other host serving an identical favicon and is one of the strongest infrastructure-clustering techniques available. Snapshots can be weeks stale, so a hit means was, not is. Shodan also sells on-demand scanning, which is active and not covered by this row.

name: SSLMate Cert Spotter
notes: Certificate Transparency search with monitoring and alerting on newly issued certificates for a domain. The monitoring angle is what distinguishes it from crt.sh: you watch an estate over the life of an engagement instead of taking one snapshot. Same structural CT blind spots apply.

name: subfinder
notes: Passive-only subdomain enumeration in default operation: queries dozens of third-party datasets and CT sources and sends nothing to the target. It also ships an opt-in active mode that resolves discovered names - selecting it changes the mode of the step and needs the same authorisation as any other active collection. Output quality tracks how many provider keys you configure - with none it falls back to a handful of free sources and under-reports badly.

name: Team Cymru IP-to-ASN Mapping
notes: Long-running free service for attributing large IP lists to origin ASN, prefix and registry without hammering RIR whois - the standard tool for bulk enrichment of log data. Query interfaces are documented on the vendor site; read the current documentation rather than reconstructing the lookup format from memory.

name: testssl.sh
notes: Local shell tool for TLS inspection: full certificate detail, SAN list, chain, protocol and cipher support. Same evidence as SSL Labs without any third party learning the target - but the connection still originates from your own host. The SAN list on a live certificate is an often-overlooked subdomain source.

name: urlscan.io (search public scans)
notes: Searchable archive of scans other people already ran: screenshots, DOM, every domain and IP the page contacted, and the certificates in use at that moment. Purely passive - you are reading someone else capture. Always check here before submitting a scan of your own.

name: urlscan.io (submit new scan)
notes: Submitting a URL makes urlscan fetch it, so the target sees a request; worse, a scan left on the default public visibility becomes searchable by anyone, including the target. Use unlisted or private visibility deliberately, or do not submit. Public scans of a target submitted by others are themselves a signal that someone else is looking.

name: ViewDNS.info
rate_limit: free web tools are throttled; API needs a key
notes: Aggregator offering reverse IP, reverse WHOIS, reverse NS and DNS history in one place. Aggregation is not corroboration: a hit here repackages someone else collection and counts as one uncorroborated lead, not two agreeing sources. The underlying data is stale and partial - never present a reverse-IP result as a complete co-hosting list, and re-verify every hit against the registry or a primary passive-DNS source before it enters findings. The same site also hosts ping, traceroute, port scan and live DNS record tools; those are active and out of scope under a passive-only mandate even though this row is graded passive for the stored-data pivots.

name: WhoisXML API
rate_limit: free tier is a small one-off credit allowance
notes: Bulk WHOIS, WHOIS history, reverse WHOIS and assorted DNS datasets behind a single key. Materially cheaper than DomainTools and adequate for generating leads, but the data is resold and re-normalised rather than observed first-hand. Aggregation is not corroboration: a field here and the same field at DomainTools may trace to one upstream collection, so agreement between them is not two independent sources. Cite the registry for anything that has to hold up.

name: AI or Not
notes: Second classifier for AI-generated images, video and audio, carried only so that a detector result can be tested against an independently built one. Same ceiling as every source in this class: high error rates in both directions, and a score never carries a finding on its own. Disagreement with Hive AI-Generated Content Detection tells you the artifact is hard to classify and that provenance work must decide the case. Agreement is not corroboration - consumer detectors train on overlapping public corpora and fail on the same compressed, upscaled and re-encoded inputs, so they fail the independence tests in 41-confidence.md.

name: Baidu Images
jurisdiction_notes: Chinese-operated; queries and uploads are processed in China and subject to local content filtering.
notes: Distinct index and the only practical reverse image route into Chinese-language sites, Weibo, Baidu Tieba and Chinese e-commerce listings. Interface is Chinese-only and results are subject to domestic censorship, so absence of a result carries less weight than elsewhere.

name: Bing Visual Search
notes: Distinct index with different crawl coverage from Google, and its region-of-interest crop tool makes it useful for querying one object inside a busy photo. Generally the weakest of the four major engines for exact-copy discovery but it surfaces pages the others miss often enough to justify the minute it takes.

name: c2patool
notes: Reference command-line reader and writer for C2PA manifests, maintained by the Content Authenticity Initiative. Development moved out of the archived contentauth/c2patool repository into the cli directory of contentauth/c2pa-rs in December 2024, so older write-ups point at a read-only repo. Prefer it over the Content Credentials web verifier for case material: it runs locally and discloses nothing, and it prints the whole manifest chain - signing certificate, claim generator, declared actions and ingredient assets - rather than a summarised verdict. It also distinguishes the four outcomes that matter: no manifest, valid manifest with a recognised signer, valid signature from an unknown or self-signed signer, and a manifest whose asset hash no longer matches the bytes. Absence of a manifest is the normal case and means nothing.

name: Content Credentials
notes: Verification of C2PA content credentials, the cryptographically signed provenance manifest that some cameras, Adobe tools and generative models now embed. When a valid manifest is present it is strong evidence of origin and edit history, including whether a generative model produced or altered the asset. Absence proves nothing at all - most files have no manifest, and manifests are stripped by most platforms on upload and by any re-encode or screenshot.

name: ExifTool
notes: The reference metadata parser and the correct first step on any file, because it runs locally and discloses nothing. Extracts GPS coordinates, capture timestamp with offset, camera make, model and serial number, lens, editing software and history, and IPTC or XMP author and contact fields. Social platforms strip most of this on upload, so an image with intact EXIF probably did not come from a public post - which is itself a finding. Metadata is trivially forged: treat it as a claim by whoever last wrote the file, graded accordingly, and corroborate GPS against imagery.

name: ffmpeg
notes: Local video toolkit, and the counterpart to ExifTool for moving images. Two jobs in this play: extract keyframes so a video becomes a set of stills that reverse image engines can actually search, and read container metadata with ffprobe - encoder handler, creation time (usually UTC and usually without an offset), rotation, stream layout and bitrate. Working on a copy already in evidence discloses nothing, which is the advantage over browser extensions that fetch frames from the hosting server. Container metadata after any platform upload describes that platform's encoder, not the recording device, so read it as a re-encode fingerprint rather than as capture data.

name: Forensically
rate_limit: none - runs client-side in the browser
notes: Browser-based image analysis suite: error level analysis, clone detection, noise analysis, luminance gradient, level sweep, principal component analysis, JPEG quantisation tables, thumbnail comparison, string extraction and a metadata reader including C2PA. Everything runs client-side and the image is never uploaded, which makes it the correct substitute for FotoForensics whenever the material is sensitive or the analysis itself must stay unobserved. The analyses carry the same interpretive hazards wherever they run: ELA and noise maps show compression and resampling history, not manipulation, and both mislead confidently on resized, screenshotted or platform-recompressed images. Treat every map as a lead that directs the next question, never as a conclusion.

name: FotoForensics
rate_limit: Free tier limits and retention differ from paid; check current terms.
jurisdiction_notes: Uploads to the free tier are publicly viewable by other users of the service. Never upload case material or anything sensitive to the free tier.
notes: Error level analysis, JPEG quantisation table and thumbnail comparison, plus a metadata view. ELA is widely misread: it highlights differing compression history, not manipulation, and clean ELA does not mean authentic while noisy ELA does not mean edited. Its practical value is the quantisation table, which fingerprints the last encoder and can contradict a claim that a file came straight from a given camera or app. Marked active, not passive: free-tier uploads are added to a publicly browsable gallery, so submitting an image publishes it where the target or anyone else can see that it is being analysed. Use the paid tier or a local tool when the analysis itself must stay unobserved.

name: Google Lens
notes: Distinct index. Strongest at recognising objects, products, landmarks, plants and embedded text, and at semantically similar rather than identical images. Weak at finding an exact reposted crop. Also performs OCR on signage in the image, which frequently solves a geolocation faster than the image match does. Uploading evidence discloses it to a third party and it may be retained - archive locally first and consider whether the upload is acceptable for the case.

name: Hive AI-Generated Content Detection
rate_limit: Free demo exists; volume use is paid - limits unknown.
notes: Classifier that scores whether an image or video was produced by a generative model. Treat every such detector as a weak signal only. Error rates are high in both directions: heavy compression, upscaling, denoising and phone beautification push authentic images toward a synthetic verdict, and current-generation models routinely evade detection. A detector score never carries a finding on its own - it directs where to look. AI or Not and Illuminarty are comparable services with different training data; disagreement between them is informative, agreement is not proof.

name: InVID WeVerify Verification Plugin
notes: Browser extension aimed at video verification: extracts keyframes from a video so they can be pushed into several reverse image engines at once, reads platform-side upload metadata, magnifies frames, and bundles a set of verification utilities. Keyframe extraction is the step that turns an unverifiable video into searchable stills. Platform API changes have repeatedly broken individual features, so confirm which modules still function. Extracting frames from a video hosted on target-controlled infrastructure fetches from that server and is not passive.

name: PimEyes
rate_limit: Free tier shows matches without source URLs; export of URLs requires a paid plan.
jurisdiction_notes: Face search is biometric processing. In the EU and UK it needs a lawful basis under GDPR and regulators have taken enforcement action against face search services; Illinois BIPA and comparable US state laws create private rights of action. Several jurisdictions effectively bar its use outside law enforcement. Confirm authority before running a query.
notes: Face search across crawled web images. Genuinely effective, which is exactly why it is legally and ethically constrained - do not use it on private individuals, and record the authority for every query. Matches are similarity scores not identifications: the false-positive rate on common facial types is real, and a match must be corroborated by an independent datapoint before it enters findings. The service offers a self-search and opt-out route, which makes it defensible for self-audit work.

name: TinEye
rate_limit: Web search is free; API access is paid - limits unknown.
notes: Distinct index built for exact and edited copies rather than semantic similarity, and the only major engine that reliably sorts results by oldest first. That makes it the tool for establishing first appearance and provenance of an image, which is the actual question in most verification work. It will not find a different photo of the same scene, and its index is much smaller than Google or Yandex.

name: Yandex Images
jurisdiction_notes: Russian-operated. The uploaded image and the query are processed in Russia.
notes: Distinct index, and consistently the strongest of the general engines for faces and for near-duplicate crops, mirrored or lightly edited copies. Far better coverage of Russian, CIS and Eastern European sites including VK and Odnoklassniki. If you run only one reverse image engine you are wrong; if you run only two, this must be one of them.

name: EU Sanctions Map
jurisdiction_notes: European Union. Presents EU restrictive measures organised by country regime with the underlying legal acts and indexes listed persons and entities. Member states implement and enforce nationally and several maintain additional national lists, so an EU-wide screen is not a member-state screen. The legally binding text is the Official Journal regulation, not this site.
notes: Use it to identify which regime and which legal act applies to a target, then read the regulation itself - aggregation is not corroboration and the Official Journal text is the citable primary. The machine-readable EU Consolidated Financial Sanctions List is distributed separately by the European Commission and has historically required a free registration to download - confirm the current access route before building anything against it. OpenSanctions carries a parsed copy of the EU list if the official feed is awkward to consume.

name: LSEG World-Check
jurisdiction_notes: Commercial risk intelligence, formerly Thomson Reuters World-Check, now part of LSEG Risk Intelligence. Contents are proprietary and licensed; profiles generally cannot be republished or shown to the subject, which matters when a finding has to be disclosed or defended. The product has a documented history of false positives and of subjects contesting entries.
notes: The de facto standard PEP and heightened-risk database in regulated KYC and AML work, and the reason a bank's screening result differs from an open-source screen on the same name. Listed here because a due-diligence report citing only free sources will be challenged by a compliance reviewer - not because its contents are verifiable from outside. Comparable products include Dow Jones Risk and Compliance, Moody's Grid and Sayari. It is a compiled secondary database and aggregation is not corroboration: treat every hit as an allegation requiring primary-source confirmation before it enters a finding. The endpoint recorded here is the product page; the database itself is behind a licence.

name: OFAC Sanctions List Search
jurisdiction_notes: United States. Covers the Specially Designated Nationals list and OFAC's non-SDN lists including sectoral sanctions, foreign sanctions evaders and correspondent-account restrictions. US sanctions carry extraterritorial effect for USD-denominated transactions and US-origin goods, so a non-US practitioner still has to screen against them.
notes: Fuzzy name matching with a similarity score, plus aliases, dates and places of birth, passport and national identity numbers, vessel IMO numbers, aircraft tail numbers and cryptocurrency addresses attached to designated persons. The 50 Percent Rule means an entity owned 50 percent or more in aggregate by designated persons is blocked without appearing on the list at all - a clean screening hit is therefore not a clean file, and ownership analysis is mandatory. Machine-readable list files are published by OFAC.

name: OpenSanctions
jurisdiction_notes: Consolidates sanctions lists from dozens of issuing bodies plus politically exposed person data, debarment lists and wanted-person notices. It is a derived dataset - legal effect always flows from the issuing authority's own list, so confirm any hit at the source before acting on it or putting it in a report.
notes: The practical way to screen one name against many regimes at once, including national lists that have no usable search interface of their own. PEP coverage is built largely from Wikidata plus curated national sources, so it is broad on national-level politicians and thin on regional officials, family members and close associates - which is exactly where PEP risk usually sits. Free for non-commercial use with bulk downloads and an API; commercial use is licensed. Entity resolution across lists is automated and produces both false merges and misses. Aggregation is not corroboration: cite the issuing authority's list, never this one.

name: UK OFSI Consolidated List
jurisdiction_notes: United Kingdom. OFSI publishes the consolidated list of financial sanctions targets under UK autonomous regimes, which diverged from the EU list after Brexit - an entity can be listed in one and not the other, and assuming equivalence is a common compliance error. Trade sanctions are administered separately by the Department for Business and Trade.
notes: The consolidated list is published as downloadable files with aliases, dates of birth, passport numbers and the statutory regime under which each target is designated. OFSI also publishes enforcement penalties and general licences, which give useful context on how strictly a regime is actually applied. UK ownership and control rules parallel the OFAC 50 percent concept but are worded differently and have been litigated - do not assume the two tests give the same answer on the same structure.

name: UN Security Council Consolidated List
jurisdiction_notes: United Nations. Individuals and entities designated under Security Council sanctions committees. UN listings take legal effect through implementation into national law by member states, so the operative instrument is the national one. National and regional lists are almost always broader than the UN list.
notes: The narrative summaries of reasons published for many listings are unusually detailed, giving aliases, dates and places of birth, passport numbers, roles and known associates - genuine investigative content rather than just a name. Published in machine-readable form. Screening only against the UN list is insufficient for virtually every compliance obligation; treat it as a baseline, not a programme. The older www.un.org path redirects to the main.un.org host recorded here.

name: US Consolidated Screening List
jurisdiction_notes: United States. Merges restricted-party lists from Treasury (OFAC), Commerce (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified List) and State (ITAR debarred, nonproliferation), which together are what a US exporter must screen against.
notes: One search covering export-control lists that OFAC's own tool does not include - the Commerce Entity List in particular catches technology-transfer risk that a purely financial sanctions screen misses entirely. Web search needs no login or key, so auth is none; the separate machine interface requires a free api.data.gov key. This is a consolidated convenience view and aggregation is not corroboration - every hit names its source list, the legal prohibition flows from that list and differs by list, and a Denied Persons hit is not an SDN hit. Read the field and confirm at the issuing agency.

name: World Bank Listing of Ineligible Firms and Individuals
jurisdiction_notes: Debarment from World Bank-financed contracts, which is a procurement exclusion rather than a financial sanction. Cross-debarment agreements mean listings by the African Development Bank, Asian Development Bank, EBRD and Inter-American Development Bank are frequently mutually recognised - check those institutions as well as this one.
notes: Names firms and individuals debarred for fraud, corruption, collusion, coercion or obstruction, with the grounds, the country and the debarment period. A debarment is a finding by an adjudicative body following an investigation and is far stronger evidence than adverse media. Affiliates are commonly listed alongside the parent, which incidentally exposes group structure that no register discloses.

name: Bing
notes: Different crawl and different ranking from Google - it routinely surfaces pages Google has dropped, and supports its own operator set. It is also the index behind DuckDuckGo and several other front ends, so agreement between those is correlation, not independent corroboration. The interface language and result set follow the requester apparent country.

name: Brave Search
rate_limit: unknown for the web interface; the separate API has a monthly free-tier cap
notes: Runs a genuinely independent index rather than reselling Bing, which makes it a real second opinion rather than a restyled one. The web interface needs no account. There is also a documented search API on a separate developer endpoint that requires a key - the practical option for scripted search that does not involve scraping a consumer engine.

name: DuckDuckGo
notes: No identity-linked query logging and no result personalisation, so two analysts get the same results - a real advantage when a finding has to be reproducible. The index is largely syndicated from Bing, so a DuckDuckGo result agreeing with a Bing result is one source seen twice, not corroboration. Bang syntax jumps straight into site-specific searches.

name: GitHub Gist
jurisdiction_notes: Content is user-published and attributable to a GitHub account rather than anonymous, but the author or a DMCA notice can remove it at any time - capture and hash anything you rely on at the moment you find it.
notes: GitHub's paste surface, and a heavier source of leaked configuration, tokens and internal hostnames than its reputation suggests, because developers use it for quick sharing outside a repository and outside whatever secret scanning covers the repository. The gap that matters: gists are a separate corpus from the repository code index, so a GitHub Code Search query never reaches them - discovery goes through a general engine's site: operator against the gist host, or through the search on the site itself. Secret gists are unlisted rather than private, are reachable by anyone holding the URL, and are not indexed, so absence proves nothing. Every gist is bound to an account, which makes the author an immediate pivot in a way an anonymous paste is not.

name: Google Search
jurisdiction_notes: Results vary by country domain and by inferred requester location; index coverage is filtered under local law, including right-to-be-forgotten delistings in the EU.
notes: Largest general index and the base for site:, inurl:, intext: and filetype: dorking. Results are personalised and not reproducible between analysts, so record the exact query string, the date, and an archived copy of every hit you rely on. Do not automate around the CAPTCHA - that is out of scope; use a paid programmable search or a different engine.

name: Intelligence X
rate_limit: free tier shows truncated previews only
jurisdiction_notes: EU-based operator. Its corpus includes leaked and breach-derived material; use of such material is restricted by CONTRACT refusal 6 and by data-protection law in most jurisdictions.
notes: Selector search across pastes, darkweb content, document leaks and historical web data. Legitimately useful for establishing that an identifier appears in publicly circulating data - which is an exposure finding. Treat a breach-derived hit as a lead about exposure, not as content to retrieve, quote or store. Graded D as an aggregator of third-party corpora of unknown handling: aggregation is not corroboration, and the same dump indexed here and elsewhere is one artefact counted twice.

name: Pastebin
rate_limit: site search is limited; the scraping API requires a paid Pro account
jurisdiction_notes: Pastes frequently contain credential dumps; use of non-public or purchased breach material is out of scope regardless of where it is hosted.
notes: Still the default drop site for configuration dumps, target lists and credential pastes. Its own search is weak - a site: query on a general engine or a paste-monitoring service works better. Unlisted pastes are never indexed, so coverage is partial by design and absence proves nothing. Content is anonymous user submission with no provenance of any kind.

name: PublicWWW
rate_limit: free tier returns a truncated result set
notes: Full-text search over the HTML, JavaScript and CSS source of crawled pages. Query an analytics or AdSense identifier, a distinctive favicon path, a wallet address or a unique code comment to surface sibling sites operated by the same party. The free tier truncates results severely and index freshness varies sharply with site popularity.

name: SearXNG
jurisdiction_notes: Public instances are operated by unrelated third parties who see every query; self-host for sensitive work.
notes: Self-hostable metasearch that aggregates many engines and strips identifying request data. searx.space lists public instances with uptime and TLS grades. Best operational security per unit of effort for general search - but using someone else instance only moves the trust problem to that operator. Graded D as an aggregator: aggregation is not corroboration, and a SearXNG result is a relayed third-party hit that has to be re-checked at the engine that produced it or at the page itself before it can be cited.

name: Yandex
jurisdiction_notes: Operated from Russia; queries and any account are subject to Russian jurisdiction. Consider what the query itself discloses before submitting a sensitive selector.
notes: Best general coverage of Russian-language and post-Soviet content, and its reverse image search consistently outperforms competitors on faces and unlabelled photographs. Weigh the operational exposure of the query against that coverage benefit before using it on a live case.

name: ADS-B Exchange
rate_limit: Public map is open; API and bulk historical access are commercial.
notes: The differentiator is that it has historically declined to filter aircraft on privacy or blocking lists, so government, military, law-enforcement surveillance and privately blocked business aircraft appear here when they are hidden on other trackers. That makes it the first tracker to check, not the last. Ownership changed in 2023 and API access moved to commercial terms - verify what remains freely available before building a workflow on it. Absence of a track usually means no receiver coverage or the transponder was off, not that the flight did not happen. The live map at globe.adsbexchange.com was reachable and open without an account at the time of check; the www homepage is marketing.

name: Equasis
rate_limit: Free registration required; intended for individual use, bulk extraction is not permitted.
jurisdiction_notes: Operated on behalf of the European Commission and participating maritime administrations. Free to use after registration; terms restrict commercial redistribution.
notes: The single most valuable free vessel source for due diligence and sanctions work. Gives registered owner, ISM manager, commercial manager and beneficial owner where declared, along with flag history, classification society, and port state control inspection and detention records. Ownership layers plus a flag change plus a name change in a short window is the classic sanctions-evasion signature, and this is where you see all three. Company entries are the pivot into corporate registry work. Data quality depends on what was declared to the reporting bodies.

name: FAA Aircraft Registry
jurisdiction_notes: Covers US-registered aircraft only. Other countries maintain separate registries with different public access - some publish owner details, others do not.
notes: Primary government record for N-registered aircraft: registered owner name and address, make, model, serial number, airworthiness and registration dates. The gotcha that matters: a large share of business aircraft are registered to owner trustees or to single-purpose LLCs, so the registered owner is frequently a trust company or a shell, not the beneficial user. Pivot that name into corporate registry work rather than reporting it as the owner. Downloadable bulk registration files exist alongside the web lookup.

name: Flightradar24
rate_limit: Free tier shows limited history; longer playback and data export require a subscription.
jurisdiction_notes: Some operators and jurisdictions restrict publication of specific aircraft movements; check before publishing.
notes: Largest crowdsourced ADS-B and MLAT receiver network with live and historical tracks, aircraft registration, type, operator and route history. Free history depth is short - the longer archive is the paid product. Honours aircraft blocking programmes, so exactly the aircraft an investigation cares about may be absent or unlabelled here while visible elsewhere. Coverage over oceans and in parts of Africa and Central Asia depends on satellite ADS-B, which is a paid data source.

name: MarineTraffic
rate_limit: Free tier shows recent positions only; track history and route playback are paid.
notes: Largest public AIS aggregator: live and historical positions, port calls, vessel particulars, IMO and MMSI numbers, and user-submitted photographs. Port call history is often more useful than the live position for establishing a pattern. AIS is self-reported and can be switched off, spoofed or set to a false identity - a gap in the track around a sanctioned port is a finding in itself, and identity spoofing between vessels sharing a name or MMSI is a known evasion technique. Terrestrial receiver coverage is coastal; open-ocean tracks depend on satellite AIS, which is the paid product. VesselFinder and FleetMon aggregate overlapping but not identical receiver networks - check a second one before concluding a vessel went dark.

name: OpenRailwayMap
jurisdiction_notes: Underlying data is ODbL licensed.
notes: Rendering of the railway tagging in OpenStreetMap: lines, gauge, electrification, signalling, sidings, yards and station infrastructure. Useful for confirming that a photographed track section matches a claimed location, for identifying industrial sidings serving a facility, and for reasoning about how material moves to a site. Completeness varies hugely by country because it depends on local mapping effort. There is no public equivalent of live flight or vessel tracking for freight rail in most countries.

name: OpenSky Network
rate_limit: Free account required for API and historical data; quotas apply and differ for research users.
jurisdiction_notes: Free use is for research and non-commercial purposes; commercial use requires a separate agreement.
notes: Research-operated ADS-B network with an unusually deep historical archive and programmatic access, which makes it the practical free option for reconstructing flights weeks or months back rather than tracking one now. Receiver coverage is concentrated in Europe and North America and is thin elsewhere. Data is raw position reports, so expect to do your own filtering and gap handling.

name: Planespotters
notes: Enthusiast-maintained registration and fleet database: serial number, build date, current and previous registrations, operators over time and dated photographs. The ownership and registration history is the useful part - it shows when an airframe changed hands or was re-registered in a different country, which is how leasing structures and sanctions evasion appear. Community-maintained, so corroborate against the national registry before treating an entry as fact.

name: UK MOT History
jurisdiction_notes: Great Britain and Northern Ireland registered vehicles only. Returns no owner or keeper details - keeper data from DVLA is released only to parties with a statutory reasonable cause. Equivalent public services exist in some other countries and not in others; most of the EU releases nothing from a plate without legal process.
notes: Government record returning make, model, colour, fuel type, first registration date and the full annual test history including dates, pass or fail, recorded mileage and advisory notes. The mileage series is the investigative value: it shows annual usage and exposes odometer inconsistency, and the advisory text sometimes describes damage. The companion DVLA vehicle enquiry service on the same domain returns tax and MOT status from a plate. Neither returns a name or address, and no legitimate OSINT route turns a UK plate into a keeper identity.

name: Google Fact Check Explorer
notes: Searches the ClaimReview markup that fact-checking organisations publish, so one query establishes whether a claim has already been adjudicated, by whom, and on what date. Use it to reach the fact-checker's evidence and the primary records they cite - never to adopt their verdict, because citing a fact-check that agrees with you is the same circular-reporting error as counting a wire story's ten republishers. Coverage skews English-language and to IFCN-signatory publishers, so absence of a fact-check is evidence about the corpus and not about the claim. Graded D as an index: grade the fact-check you land on, and cite the record it rests on.

name: Wikipedia
notes: Never citable for a claim - cite the reference it cites, after reading that reference. The investigative value is the per-page revision history, an append-only dated record of when each sentence entered the article and which account added it, which is how citogenesis is detected: an unsourced claim added here, picked up by an outlet, then cited back into the article as independent corroboration. Compare the revision timestamp against the outlet publication date before counting them as two sources. Talk pages preserve the disputes the article text smooths over, and are often the fastest route to the strongest counter-argument.

name: Blockchair
notes: Multi-chain block explorer with one search box that runs a query across every chain it indexes at once - Bitcoin and several of its forks, Ethereum and a range of others; read the current chain list on the site rather than assuming coverage. That cross-chain search is the reason to reach for it first: an 0x address is simultaneously valid on every EVM chain and the same key controls it on all of them, so a single-chain explorer showing no activity establishes nothing. Use it to find which chains an address actually transacted on, then read the detail on that chain's own explorer. A WAF returns 401 to scripted requests, so it is not agent-fetchable; it loads normally in a browser.

name: Blockstream.info
notes: Bitcoin block explorer operated by Blockstream on the open-source Esplora codebase, with separate views for testnet and the Liquid sidechain. It is the one Bitcoin explorer in this registry that answers plain scripted HTTP with no bot challenge, so it is what an agent can actually read; mempool.space is better for mempool and fee state but discourages programmatic volume. Shows inputs, outputs, spent status, script types and raw transaction bytes - the raw form matters because retrieving it lets you check the transaction hash yourself instead of trusting the indexer. It does no wallet clustering and applies no entity labels, which is a feature here: what it returns is a claim about the ledger and never about who controls an address.

name: OpenSea
notes: The largest NFT marketplace. Its investigative value is the profile layer rather than the art: an address with marketplace activity often has a profile carrying a chosen username, a bio and sometimes a linked website or social account, which turns a bare address into a named social lead worth pivoting to osint-identity. Holdings and transfer history are rendered from the chain and are as good as the chain; the profile fields are self-reported by whoever controls the address, are graded as self-report and never as identity, and can be set by an impersonator who registered a lookalike name. Holding a token is also not choosing it - anyone can send an NFT or token to any address, and spam airdrops are constant. Front end is a JavaScript application so it is not agent-fetchable; the documented API requires a key.
